domain: human-in-the-loop workflow ergonomics / repeated ratification design
axioms: A single pilot measurement of a human workflow does not by itself establish the cost or tolerability of repeating that workflow at scale, especially across heterogeneous instances.
Distinct cognitive operations (ratifying a pre-drafted claim vs. originating new content from nothing) have different costs and should not be collapsed into one aggregate time figure.
All-or-nothing approval gates (must resolve every item before the gate opens) are prone to end-of-session fatigue and rubber-stamping, a well-documented failure mode in long-form review workflows.
A workflow's real-world sustainability depends on its recurring, interrupt-driven cadence, which a focused single-sitting pilot does not necessarily reproduce.

An easy override or escape hatch sitting next to a costly mandatory step changes the incentive structure enough that the measured cost of the 'proper' path may not reflect what participants actually do.
The representativeness of the pilot subject (its resourcing, incentives, existing material) bounds how far its measured cost can be generalized.
primitives: per-unit cost extrapolated to population size
failure_mode: May underweight whether the format's own representation (schema, validator contract) is internally sound, focusing purely on the human task around it.
Could over-index on measurement-methodology critique and under-attend to whether the six fields themselves are the right things to be confirming.
Is not well positioned to judge whether the whole card-and-gate apparatus addresses the estate's actual overwhelm problem, only whether the specific human step is workable.
May assume ergonomic problems it flags are load-bearing even when the goal's actual near-term scope (one confirm) makes them premature.
